title: Manna (Exodus 16)
hookLine: bread every morning, just enough, and it spoils if hoarded

lines: IF ONLY WE'D DIED IN EGYPT.
cards: One month out of Egypt, the singing has stopped. They're in the desert, the food is gone, and the whole community complains to Moses and Aaron.
If only we'd died in Egypt, they say, where we sat by the pots of meat and ate bread till we were full. A month ago they were slaves making bricks without straw. Now Egypt is a buffet.
Hunger rewrites the past fast. And God's answer to the complaining isn't a lecture. It's breakfast.

teach.b: First, the bread. In the morning, when the dew lifts, there's something on the ground, fine and flaky, like frost. The people look at it and say to each other, man hu, what is it?
That question became its name: manna, the what-is-it. It was white like coriander seed, the text says, and tasted like wafers made with honey. Second, the rule.
Gather what you need, an omer a person. And something strange: whoever gathered much had nothing left over, and whoever gathered little had no lack.
Leave none of it till morning, Moses says. Some keep it anyway, just in case. By morning it's crawling with worms and it stinks.
Third, the rest. On the sixth day they gather double, and that portion keeps through the Sabbath. Some go out on the seventh day anyway, and find nothing.
Bread for today, every day, for forty years. Fourth, where Catholics hear it.
In John's Gospel, Jesus says the fathers ate manna in the desert, and then: I am the living bread come down from heaven.
The Church sings at Benediction before the Blessed Sacrament: you gave them bread from heaven, with all sweetness in it, words drawn from the Book of Wisdom.
And in the Our Father, Matthew uses a rare Greek word for bread, epiousios, and readers still debate exactly what it means. Daily? For tomorrow?
The Douay-Rheims, following Saint Jerome's Latin, translates it supersubstantial bread. The Catechism reads it both ways at once: today's food, and the Eucharist.

how: At Benediction of the Blessed Sacrament, many parishes sing the versicle "You have given them bread from heaven," drawn from Wisdom 16:20, and Catholics pray for daily bread in the Our Father at every Mass.

games.q: you're in the desert with a jar of manna left from today. Moses said leave none of it till morning. you keep some anyway, just in case. what do you find at dawn?
o: it's full of worms and it stinks.
games.why: it bred worms and stank. the bread was for today. only the Sabbath portion kept overnight.

practice: Notice anything you're carrying ahead in your head, tomorrow's worries, next month's bills, next week's argument: that's manna kept overnight.
Set it down for now and ask simply, what do I need for today, enough food, enough patience, enough strength for one hard conversation?
If you pray, use the line from the Our Father, give us this day our daily bread; if you don't, name today's need and let tomorrow's wait.

wordCard.voice: Manna. From the Hebrew question man hu, what is it? Bread in the desert every morning, enough for one day. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: what is it? the people's question that became the bread's name, manna.

carryVoice: Your line: daily bread. Enough for today, every day, and none left to hoard. Until tomorrow.
